title: Create Custom Outfits For Inzoi Using Clo Everywear
description:
Learn step by step how to create amazing custom garments for the inZOI game using CLO EveryWear! In this video, we show you how to use CLO's EveryWear features to easily optimize your garments, then export them using the Inzoi Modkit, and finally, share your mod to other users through CONNECT Gamewear.

📌Female: https://connect.clo-set.com/detail/951e18201cfe47b3a23b95fa62bd0aca
📌Male: https://connect.clo-set.com/detail/c8c285f9616d410cb4cc084544a6c917
📌Everywear Tutorial: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S72i-Y9nJoA
📌Inzoi Modkit: https://mod-docs.playinzoi.com/ModKit/How-to/Getting-Started/01install.html
📌Masking System: https://mod-docs.playinzoi.com/ModKit/project/CAZ/Guide/03.%20Masking%20System.html
📌CONNECT: https://connect.clo-set.com/
transcript: Hello everyone, my name is Gabriele Bercotti and I'm a specialist in 3D design and implementation at Claw. In this tutorial, we will show you how to use Claw Everywhere to create clothes for the game in ZOI. Let's go to the video! The first step is to download the assets provided in the Connect Store. You'll find the links in the description below. Make sure to download the entire folder and unzip it as it contains several assets which you'll be using through the process. I like linking my folders in the Claw Library so I can quickly access the assets whenever I need them. Once you open the files, you'll notice that both avatars have red lines along the wrists. This indicates that the garment sleeves should not extend beyond that point. For pants, ensure that they do not touch the ground. Additionally, the female avatar has a red area along the hips, which means skirts should ideally not go below this line, as doing so makes the rigging process more challenging. Here I have a three-piece look that I prepared specifically to demonstrate various scenarios and best practices when preparing a garment for a video game. Video games generally require maximum asset optimization. So if you have a garment that is true to life, with all the patterns, finishes and details, we will need to adjust it to ensure better rigging and optimization inside the game. Take this cardigan as an example. It has folded cuffs and hem, just like in real life. To adapt it to the game, I will cut and remove half of the patterns. To add realism to the patterns, we will use additional thickness rendering. But first, make sure you are using the thick textured surface option in the 3D window toggle menu. I'll start by selecting the cardigan cuffs and hemline and adding 5 millimeters of thickness. This creates the effect of two layers of fabric, which is what I want. I'll do the same for the placket. Next, I'll hide the cardigan to work on the bodysuit. Since this piece won't be very visible, I don't need to worry too much about the armholes. However, if I wanted to use this garment without the jacket in the insole later, I would recommend increasing its additional thickness rendering to 3 millimeters. I'll apply the same logic to the shorts, increasing the thickness of patterns that represent double layers or that are generally thicker. Now I'll bring the cardigan back. Before moving on to every wear, there's one more quick step. Since my file is currently in high resolution, I will increase the particle distance to 8 and change the additional thickness collision to 2.5 millimeters to ensure the garment remains stable during simulation. Finally, I'll activate the wireframe so you can see the mesh. For better rigging results, it's ideal to have a quad mesh. Fortunately, Claw has a special algorithm that converts the mesh to quads, while keeping it optimized and respecting the garment's curvature. So I'll select all the patterns with Ctrl A, then I'll right-click and change the mesh type to Quad. Before running the optimization, here's a useful tip. Reduce the poly count by adjusting the resolution of the pattern edges. By default, this value is set to 6, so I'll select all my patterns and lower it to 2, since in most areas this won't be noticeable. Next, using the Edit Pattern tool, I can manually adjust areas where I want higher resolution, such as the cardigan placket, which I'll set to 4. I'll do the same adjustment to some of the hemlines. Now it's time to open Everywhere. Start by selecting a pattern, then Connect, then Everywhere. Once the window opens, you'll see the avatar and garment polygon count displayed in both the 3D window and in the Everywhere panel. The number we need to focus on is the garment polygons. For Enzoi, we recommend a maximum of 15,000 quads for looks that contain top and bottom, and 20,000 quads for looks that contain top, bottom, and outerwear. Before running the optimization, we strongly recommend converting all of your top stitches from OBJ to Texture. Since top stitches account for a significant portion of the total polygon count in this project, switching them to Texture will greatly reduce the overall number of garment polygons. I'll set my goal to 30,000 quads, which is slightly higher than the 20K limit, because I know I'll use other tools later, to reduce it further. Now click Optimize, and Qua will increase the particle distance of the garment to help us reach the target. If you prefer, instead of using Everywhere optimization, you can manually adjust the particle distance for each pattern individually. This approach gives you greater control over the garment, allowing you to decide which areas require higher resolution, and where a lower mesh density is acceptable. When you use Everywhere optimization tool, it transforms all trims into plain type, meaning each trim is now represented by a flat surface with a texture, like you can see here with this button. If a trim is close to the avatar's face, and might be seen up close, you may want to revert it to a mesh type. To do this, click the trim in the object profile, and uncheck Plain. Then manually you can reduce the poly count. I'll set mine to 500, which should be enough for this button. For less noticeable trims, like the belt buckle, I'll leave them as plain type. Next, we need to mask out parts that won't be visible in the game. For example, the lower and back sections of the bodysuit will be hidden by the shorts and cardigan, so we can mask those out. Click the paintbrush icon to start masking. I prefer working in the 2D window, but you can also hide parts in the 3D view. Note that the 2D window has front and back tabs, so you can choose which side of the mesh to hide. Since I want to hide the mesh on both sides of the fabric, I'll select the double-sided brush option, and then I can paint the areas of the patterns that I know will not appear in the game, as the lower part of the bodysuit and the back pattern. We can also mask the internal mesh of patterns to reduce even more the poly count. I'll uncheck the double-sided brush, switch to back view, and select enclosed region. Then I can select the inner mesh of patterns that won't be visible during the gameplay, like the sleeves. Don't mask areas like the shorts' hems, as they might be visible from certain angles. Once you finish, you can select exit. As you can see, these steps allowed us to reduce the poly count while maintaining the garment's high quality. Next, we'll use the auto-seal tool to ensure a clean finish in areas that can be closed. Here, I'll hide my avatar using the Shift-A shortcut, so we can get a better view of the garment's internal part. Then, I can choose between the disc or 3D pen option. They work very similarly. With the disc option, imagine you're sealing the sleeve with a circular shape. You simply need to click on three points that will define where the disc will be created. Next, Claw will ask you to pick one of the sides of the mesh you want to seal. I'll select the bottom part, and now you can see that Claw has sealed the sleeve opening. This guarantees a cleaner finish when we bring the avatar back, and ensures that areas with foul polygons won't be visible inside during gameplay. Please note that the applied auto-seal can only be viewed in the 3D window when using the thick textured surface mode, and any non-visible inner mesh of the pattern will be automatically masked. Since we won't be simulating Claw physics in real time, we need to read the garment so it moves according to the avatar's movements. You can start by clicking on Apply. Next, we need to check if the garment looks correct during different avatar motions. Go back to the library, and inside the Assets folder, you'll find the Motion folder. Double-click it to apply. Then go to the Animation menu, and open the Animation Editor. First, right-click on the timeline, and select Clamp Range to Active Frames, so we can watch the entire animation. Then hit Play, and analyze whether the garment behaves correctly. Here we are looking for parts of the garment that aren't moving with the avatar, areas where the mesh is colliding with the body or other fabrics, and regions around the joints that appear unnatural. After the first animation, we return to Frame 1 and check the second motion. This motion will stretch the avatar's body, so we can verify whether the weights are evenly distributed after rigging. We have several other tools that can assist during the rigging and weight painting process, and you can learn more about them in our Everywhere tutorial, which will be linked in the description below. As everything looks correct, we can now click on Switch to Bind Pose and move on to the next step. Now we can move to the Material tab in Everywhere. Before clicking Package, I recommend selecting all the patterns and in your Property Editor, choosing Side Face under UV Expansion. This will ensure that our texture extends to the sides of the patterns. I will also increase the seam size to 8 and then select Pack UVs. If you have large patterns that won't appear in the game, such as the bodysuit back, you can slightly reduce the size before running the UV pack, this will guarantee a higher resolution for patterns that will actually be visible in the game. Finally, you can click Exit. The next step is Baking. Click Apply next to Baking to generate the maps. Here we will generate the detailed Normal Map and Ambient Occlusion maps. They will guarantee a higher resolution effect in your garment without compromising the polygon count. Before moving on, make sure to save a good thumbnail image of your garment as it will be used later on. Now we can finally click Export and type in our garment's name. In the Export options, make sure you select Insoi as the platform and choose Fick Object. If your garment has any type of opacity, select the Armor option. I would be able to select the Arm option if I hadn't set my buckle trim as a plane. Since it uses a PNG texture, I need to go with the Armor option. Now I can click OK. Just keep in mind, before exporting, you need to ensure all your patterns are rigged and that all your UVs are packed within a single tile. Otherwise, you'll see an error message when you click the Export button. One more step is needed before we can bring our garment into the game. This will be done using the Mod Kit provided by Insoi. You can download it using the link in the description or by searching for Insoi Mod Kit in your Epic Games app and clicking to download it. Once the download is complete, open the Mod Kit. We will start by duplicating an existing garment to use as the base for our mod. Select Create a Zoi, then change the dropdown to Set. Use the checkboxes for Male, Female, Adult and Youth to filter assets according to the garment you created. I recommend choosing the garment that most closely resembles your design, as this will make masking body parts easier later. Since my outfit has shorts and long sleeves, I'll use this jumpsuit as the base. Click the arrow and select Create New Mod Project. Add a name and description for your mod, then click Create. A new folder will be generated for your project. Next, click the arrow next to your newly created mod and select Open Mod Workspace. A window will appear asking if you want to create a copy of the source asset data. Then click Copy. Now, we will replace the current garment with our own mesh and textures. Scroll down and click Open Resource Import Tool. This special window allows you to import assets in a standardized way. First, ensure Skeletal Mesh Outfit is selected. Drag and drop the FBX file exported from Glow and wait for it to load. Then, move on to the textures. Click the Base Color button and drag and drop the base color image. Repeat this process for the normal, arm, and thumbnail images. After that, close the Resource Import Tool. You'll notice new folders called Mesh and Texture inside your project folder. Start by opening the Mesh folder and selecting the garment file you just imported. Scroll up to where the current mesh is listed and click the arrow icon to replace the jumpsuit with the file you selected in the object browser. Now, we need to add a new material for this outfit. Start by clicking the MiCast button and typing the name of your material. Click the arrow next to it to reveal the slots where we will add our maps. Next, go to the Textures folder, select the arm texture, and then click the arrow to apply this image as the map. Repeat the same process for the normal and base color maps. Now our texture is set, but we still need to apply it to the garment mesh. First, click the Mesh icon and click to the folder icon next to your material. This will take you to its location inside the project folder. Then double-click the mesh asset to open its editor. In the material slot, click the arrow icon to apply the newly created material to the mesh. Finally, save and close this window. Since I also imported my thumbnail image, I'll navigate to the Textures folder, select the thumbnail, and apply it to the thumbnail slot. We are almost ready. The last step is to make sure the body regions being masked out are correct. This is important to avoid collisions and improve game performance. Ensoy uses a group ID system that makes it easy for users to hide specific body parts. Under the Body Hiding section, you'll see which areas are masked based on the garment we selected as the base earlier. Scroll up and click Enable Body Region Hiding. This option gives you a preview of the parts that will be hidden during the game. Since I started with a jumpsuit, my mask is already correct. As you can see, the visible areas of the body display the colorful texture which represents the body mask in the Masking Region Guide. I'll hide the garment preview so you can see that all body areas covered by the garment are masked out. But let's imagine that my garment was a short-sleeved t-shirt. In that case, I would scroll down and instead of Arms All, I would choose Arms All Short, so the avatar arms would remain visible in the game. If you need more details about Insoi's body hiding system, I'll leave a link in the description with a more detailed explanation. Now I'll return to the original preview settings, then click Save and select the arrow to go back to my projects. To test a mod on your computer, click the arrow next to your project and select Create Local Mod Pattern. Click Save. Save the file in the 88849 folder located inside the Mods folder in Insoi's documents. The mods will still work within the main Mods folder, but for better management, we recommend placing them in the 88849 folder. Then wait until you see the pop-up message Packaging Successful. Now you can launch Insoi. Just make sure to check if the mods are available. Go to OptionsMods and make sure that Enable Mods option is turned on. Next, enter the Character Studio. Choose the avatar type and open the Outfit tab. Go to Sets, scroll down until you find your outfit and click to wear it. All your created outfits will have a mod icon next. Now that we have confirmed our mod is working properly, we can share it through the Connect Gamewear platform. This allows other players to access your creations and use them in their own game. First, navigate to the folder where we just saved the package file. Select the folder you want to upload and compress it into a zip file. Next, we will upload our garment into Gamewear. Start by logging into Connect and clicking the Upload button. On the Upload screen, select Gamewear. Then, in Windows File Explorer, select the zip file of the outfit you want to upload. Here, you can add the name, the description, tags and other images to your file. Then, we can set the garment category for our item. Adding categories will improve the item compatibility and search results, since users can search and filter items by category. In the Recolor option, select Unavailable, since we haven't created a RGB mask map that would allow us to recolor garments inside Enzoi. For pricing options, the pricing feature is currently unavailable, and only free items are allowed. Then, click Publish to make the item public. You can also click Draft to keep the item hidden from other users while allowing further editing or reuploading. You can view your uploaded items under the Gamewear tab in your profile. And that's it! We just finished creating our Enzoi mod using Claw Everywhere tools, Enzoi Mod Kit and Gamewear, so you can share your creations with friends. I hope you enjoyed this tutorial and see you next time! Thanks for watching!
